section_summary: This section covers U.S. diplomatic reporting on proceedings and debates in the Japanese Imperial Diet from February 1940 through March 1941. The primary focus of early 1940 is the political crisis triggered by representative Takao Saito's critical interpellation challenging government policy in China, which resulted in his expulsion and accelerated efforts to form a monolithic political structure. Coverage from late 1940 and early 1941 details the opening of the 76th Diet under the Imperial Rule Assistance framework, featuring addresses by Premier Fumimaro Konoye and Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka defending the Tripartite Pact, managing relations with the United States and the Soviet Union, and centralizing wartime economic control.

subfiles.about: Reports the reopening of the Imperial Diet and summarizes policy addresses by Premier Yonai and Foreign Minister Arita.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Diet reopened after a 35-day recess with major addresses by Premier Yonai and the Ministers for Foreign Affairs, War, and Navy. Yonai reiterated policies of non-involvement in the European war, support for Wang Ching-wei's proposed central government in China, and adjustment of relations with third powers. Grew notes that Foreign Minister Arita's speech was cabled in full to Washington for distribution by the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.title: Diet Reopening and Speeches of Premier Yonai and Foreign Minister Arita

subfiles.about: Reports German press commentary on Foreign Minister Arita's Diet speech.
subfiles.summary: The Berlin press commented on Foreign Minister Arita's Diet speech, capitalizing on his remarks concerning the origin of the European war and British interference with Japanese shipping. German commentators welcomed Arita's appreciation of relations with Germany and Italy under the Anti-Comintern Pact. The press emphasized common opposition to foreign provocation and noted Japan's pursuit of a new order in East Asia parallel to German efforts in Europe.
subfiles.title: German Press Reaction to Arita's Diet Address

subfiles.about: Summarizes unfavorable Japanese editorial reaction to Foreign Minister Arita's opening address to the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports uniformly critical Japanese newspaper reaction to Foreign Minister Arita's Diet speech. Papers including Chugai, Kokumin, Yomiuri, Hochi, and Asahi characterized the speech as vague, spiritless, and contradictory in seeking general appeasement while attempting to establish a new order. The press concluded that the address demonstrated an inability to confront the serious international situation.
subfiles.title: Japanese Press Reaction to Diet Opening Address

subfiles.about: Reports on Takao Saito's Lower House speech attacking Japan's China policy and the resulting political controversy.
subfiles.summary: Diet member Takao Saito delivered an outspoken speech in the Lower House attacking the government's China policy, resulting in portions being expunged from the record and placed under a press ban. Saito questioned whether settling the conflict on the basis of the Konoye Declaration would render sacrifices futile and cast doubt on the viability of the proposed Wang Ching-wei regime. In the expunged portion, Saito suggested abandoning the refusal to deal with Chiang Kai-shek and derided describing the conflict as a holy war, prompting the Minister of War to plan a rebuttal.
subfiles.title: Interpellation of Takao Saito in the Lower House

subfiles.about: Reports Chinese press commentary from Chungking on Takao Saito's Diet interpellation.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Peck reports Chinese newspaper commentary in Chungking regarding Takao Saito's February 2 speech in the Japanese Diet. Leading journals such as Hsing Shu Pao, Ta Kung Pao, and Sao Tang Pao analyzed the speech as evidence of growing war-weariness and political division within Japan. The Hankow Herald remarked that the incident demonstrated that Japanese parliamentarianism was effectively dead.
subfiles.title: Chinese Press Comment on Takao Saito's Diet Speech

subfiles.about: Reports that Diet proceedings on February 8 focused on domestic matters rather than foreign affairs.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew briefly informs the Department of State that proceedings in the Diet on February 8 focused on domestic issues. Little attention was paid to foreign affairs during that session.
subfiles.title: Diet Proceedings on Domestic Problems

subfiles.about: Analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 4491 regarding Takao Saito's Diet interpellation and broader political cleavage in Japan.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Cabot Coville)
subfiles.summary: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluates Tokyo Despatch No. 4491 concerning Takao Saito's speech. The memorandum concurs with the Embassy that Saito voiced concerns widely felt by the Japanese public regarding government policy in China. It concludes that significant political realignments in Japan will depend on how openly the Army chooses to assert its political role and accept responsibility.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Despatch No. 4491

subfiles.about: Transmits a comprehensive report and press clipping on Takao Saito's Diet interpellation and the resulting political upheaval.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an extensive review of Minseito member Takao Saito's February 2 interpellation in the Diet questioning the indefinite duration of the China Incident, the meaning of the New Order in East Asia, and the terms of the Konoye statement. Saito's derision of the term holy war sparked intense backlash from military delegates and nationalist factions, prompting the expunging of his remarks, his resignation from the Minseito, and referral to a disciplinary committee. Enclosed is a Japan Advertiser clipping covering the debate, including interpellations by Dr. Minoru Togo and replies by Premier Yonai, Foreign Minister Arita, and War Minister Hata.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4491: Mr. Takao Saito's Interpellation in the Diet

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 4602 on Takao Saito's expulsion and political realignments in Japan.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Cabot Coville)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Despatch No. 4602 detailing the unanimous committee recommendation and subsequent closed-session vote of the Diet on March 7 to expel Takao Saito. The memorandum emphasizes that Saito's speech and its aftermath clarified an underlying political cleavage between hardline military expansionists and moderates who preferred more orderly methods of securing dominance in East Asia. It notes that growing domestic economic strain and continued Chinese resistance fueled latent sympathy for Saito's views.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Despatch No. 4602

subfiles.about: Reports the events leading to Takao Saito's expulsion from the Diet and encloses a translated text of his expunged remarks.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details political maneuvering surrounding Takao Saito's expulsion from the Diet on March 7, 1940, noting strong underlying sympathy for Saito's realistic critique across party lines. The despatch analyzes factional dynamics within the Minseito, Seiyukai, and Shakai Taishuto, as well as the emerging movement to form a unified pro-military party. Enclosed is an English translation from the Osaka Mainichi of Saito's expunged remarks, which criticized utopian formulas, questioned the material power of the Wang Ching-wei regime, and urged fair distribution of wartime burdens.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4602: Mr. Takao Saito's Diet Interpellation: Expulsion of Mr. Saito

subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of Despatch No. 994 to Peiping concerning Takao Saito's Diet speech.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Caldwell transmits to the Secretary of State a copy of his Despatch No. 994 to the American Embassy in Peiping. The enclosed communication concerns an editorial discussing Takao Saito's controversial speech in the Japanese Diet.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1282: Transmission of an Editorial on the Diet Speech of Mr. Takao Saito

subfiles.about: Transmits and analyzes a Peking and Tientsin Times editorial discussing Takao Saito's speech and wartime realism.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Caldwell forwards an editorial entitled "The Tangled Web" from the February 16, 1940 issue of the Peking and Tientsin Times. The editorial reflects on the controversy stirred by Saito and Reikichi Kita when demanding definitions of slogans like Hakko Ichiu and the New Order in East Asia. It argues that modern total war inexorably dictates political and collectivist economic transformations regardless of the intentions of statesmen or the formulas of initial declarations.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 994: Transmission of an Editorial on the Diet Speech of Mr. Takao Saito

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 4611 regarding February 1940 Diet proceedings.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Tokyo Despatch No. 4611, dated March 27, 1940, covering Diet proceedings in February 1940. The original paper is filed under 894.00 P.R./147.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Diet Proceedings: February, 1940

subfiles.about: Extract from a Tokyo Embassy monthly political report reviewing February 1940 Diet proceedings and the Saito controversy.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Section III of the Tokyo Embassy's political report covers the reopening of the Diet on February 1 and reviews speeches by Premier Yonai and Foreign Minister Arita. It highlights Takao Saito's February 2 interpellation questioning the indefinite prosecution of the China conflict and the practical value of the Konoye principles. The report details the ensuing political uproar, right-wing and military pressure demanding Saito's expulsion for deriding the holy war, and his refusal to resign his seat voluntarily.
subfiles.title: Political Report Extract: Internal Political Conditions: Diet (February 1940)

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo press commentary on the convocation of the 76th session of the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reviews editorial comment on the opening of the 76th Diet session following the dissolution of traditional political parties. Japanese newspapers expressed apprehension over potential friction between parliamentarians and the newly established Imperial Rule Assistance Association. Editorials in Asahi and Hochi urged Diet members to maintain an active constitutional role rather than functioning as passive robots under the new structure.
subfiles.title: Press Commentary on Convocation of 76th Imperial Diet

subfiles.about: Reports in four sections on the opening addresses to the 76th Diet by Premier Konoye and Foreign Minister Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a four-part summary of speeches delivered at the reopening of the 76th Diet session. Premier Konoye appealed for a national defense state, public support for the Imperial Rule Assistance movement, and domestic economic mobilization. Foreign Minister Matsuoka defended the Tripartite Pact, surveyed relations with China, the Soviet Union, and Southeast Asia, and criticized American export embargoes and defense concepts while maintaining an unexpectedly temperate tone toward the United States.
subfiles.title: Opening Addresses to the 76th Diet by Premier Konoye and Foreign Minister Matsuoka

subfiles.about: Reports Japanese press commentary on Foreign Minister Matsuoka's address to the Diet.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo vernacular newspapers generally approved Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Diet speech while emphasizing the gravity of the diplomatic crisis facing Japan. Chugai viewed the address as an effective response to American leadership, while Asahi criticized Matsuoka for an overly conciliatory posture toward the Soviet Union and failure to explain Axis delays in recognizing the Nanking government. Editorials advocated reinforcing national defense rather than attempting to curry favor with foreign powers.
subfiles.title: Press Reactions to Matsuoka's Diet Address

subfiles.about: Reports Pravda's brief coverage of the opening of the Japanese Diet and Premier Konoye's address.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Steinhardt reports from Moscow that the Soviet newspaper Pravda noted the opening of the Japanese Parliament without editorial comment. The paper published a brief, factual summary of Premier Konoye's speech based on dispatches from the Domei News Agency.
subfiles.title: Pravda Coverage of Japanese Diet Opening

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 102 regarding statements by Diet members on conciliation with the United States.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 102, dated January 22, 1941, filed under 711.94/1925. The telegram reported remarks made by three Diet members at an America-Japan Society gathering indicating a policy of conciliation toward the United States.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Japanese Government Policy toward the United States

subfiles.about: Reports Pravda's publication of a summary of Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Diet address.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Steinhardt informs Washington that Pravda carried a Tass report from Tokyo summarizing Foreign Minister Matsuoka's speech at the opening of the Diet. The Soviet report focused primarily on Matsuoka's remarks concerning Soviet-Japanese diplomatic and fisheries relations, omitting editorial commentary.
subfiles.title: Pravda Summary of Matsuoka's Diet Speech

subfiles.about: Reports the Cabinet's decision to halve the legislative program submitted to the Diet session.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that following a Cabinet conference, the Japanese Government decided to reduce the number of bills introduced during the Diet session by half. Bills dropped included election and local government reforms, while priority was placed on measures centralizing economic control, notably the revision of the National General Mobilization Law and the Peace Maintenance Law. The decision was described as a concession to the House of Representatives in exchange for prohibiting interpellations of Cabinet ministers.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Reduction of Legislative Program in the Diet

subfiles.about: Reports conversations with Foreign Minister Matsuoka and his secretary regarding access to Diet committee records.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew recounts discussions with Foreign Minister Matsuoka, who expressed annoyance over inaccurate foreign reporting of his Diet committee remarks and offered to make transcripts available. Subsequent consultation with Matsuoka's secretary, Toshikazu Kase, revealed that official transcripts could not be produced within two or three days and were treated as strictly confidential by the Diet. Grew concludes that foreign diplomats must continue to rely on vernacular press reports, leaving the situation unimproved.
subfiles.title: Availability of Diet Committee Records to Diplomatic Corps

subfiles.about: Reports scheduled secret plenary sessions of the Diet to hear reports on foreign policy and Southeast Asian negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that both houses of the Diet were scheduled to convene in a secret plenary session on March 15 to hear reports on foreign policy, particularly negotiations concerning Thailand and French Indochina. This marked the first Diet meeting called since the recess that began on March 2.
subfiles.title: Secret Plenary Session of Diet on Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Official text of Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka's address at the opening of the 76th session of the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: An official English translation distributed by the Japanese Embassy of Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka's address to the 76th Imperial Diet. Matsuoka outlined Japan's foreign policy within the spirit of Hakko Ichiu and detailed the operation of the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy. He reviewed diplomatic and economic negotiations with China, the Netherlands East Indies, French Indochina, Thailand, and the Soviet Union, while warning the United States that its export embargoes and broad defense perimeter threatened peace in the Pacific.
subfiles.title: Address by Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka at the Opening of the 76th Session of the Imperial Diet
